+The browser overlays the procedural fly and a pistol extruded from the native
+weapon pixels. The grip, barrel and muzzle flash inherit the fly's position,
+heading and the engine's aiming pitch; they never billboard toward the camera.
+First-person HUD offsets (sx/sy) are not applied to the fly's grip. Pistol depth
+is an illustrative interpretation because Doom supplies 2D weapon artwork, not
+a 3D gun. Native frame changes are retained; crossed flash planes are visible
+only when the engine supplies a muzzle-flash frame. Enemies, textures,
+projectiles and impact effects remain rendered by Doom. No bullets, attacks,
+hits or enemies are invented. Wings are decorative. Avatar occlusion has a
+small tolerance because the native 8-bit depth is approximate.
+
+Frontend regression checks cover translated/rotated grip and muzzle transforms,
+engine pitch, independence from camera orientation and HUD sway, volumetric
+weapon geometry, and flash removal when the native flash layer disappears.
+This presentation fix does not change the engine, neural controller or learning.

↳NEXT FRAME. SAME BRAIN. REPEAT.Diagrams are schematics, not live data.

MONSTERS DON’T CLOCK OUT.

Four monsters start the round. More arrive, up to four imps and four bullet-firing zombies. Separate caps keep slow survivors from blocking the other type’s replacements. Ammo boxes respawn after collection; kills also drop ammo. Death resets the arena and ammunition. No time limit.

The neural state carries on between rounds. These are engineered Doom rules; the fly still supplies every turn, move and shot through the same fixed neural mapping. Arena v1 allowed a circling stalemate; v2’s results are recorded separately. Longer survival alone is not evidence of learning.

MEMORY

TAKE A HIT. UPDATE THE WIRING.

Nonfatal damage schedules a 200 ms artificial stimulus into two PPL101 dopamine cells. Their spikes and recent Kenyon-cell activity update the strength of 4,184 existing KC→MBON11 connections. Game health never chooses actions or directly sets a weight.

The rule can strengthen or weaken connections; its timing traces, bounds and gradual decay are modeling choices informed by fly memory research. Other connection strengths and the button mapping stay fixed. Memory and neural state carry across rounds. Terminal damage is excluded, and pending feedback stops at reset.

Experimental training is running. Getting better is unproven. The earlier candidate failed conditioning and visual-recovery checks, and its small survival pilot included worse outcomes after training. Changed weights and longer rounds alone are not evidence of learning. See the failed tests and controls ↗ · Exact live protocol ↗

YOU GET THE CAMERA. THE BRAIN KEEPS THE CONTROLLER.

The 3D camera uses Doom’s own renderer: the same arena, Freedoom textures, enemy sprites, projectiles and impacts as the first-person view. A separate observer engine follows the exact game actions. Its first-person pixels, counters and object states must match the primary engine after every tick; a mismatch disables the camera.

The fly is an illustrated 3D avatar at the player’s position and heading. It holds the original weapon artwork, including the engine’s actual firing and muzzle-flash frames. Doom uses 2D sprites in a 3D world, so the weapon and monsters retain that style. Wings are decorative; the player still moves along the ground. Avatar occlusion uses an approximate depth buffer.

Your camera only requests another rendering of the current state. It never advances the game or enters the brain’s sensory input, reinforcement or controls. The 3D view has its own synchronized counters and can be slightly ahead of the buffered first-person stream. Recording at 30 video frames per second does not speed up the brain or invent actions.
